lines: A bike maker borrows by selling a bond: you pay one thousand dollars today. It pays you five percent, fifty dollars, every year for three years, then hands back your thousand.
That thousand is the face value, or par. The fifty dollar yearly payment is the coupon. The date your thousand comes back is maturity.
Now new bonds start paying seven percent. Nobody pays a full thousand for your five percent bond anymore. Its price falls until a buyer earns seven percent: to about nine hundred forty seven dollars.
That's the bond seesaw. When interest rates go up, bond prices go down. When rates fall to three percent, the same bond is worth about one thousand fifty seven dollars, a premium.
Longer bonds swing more. A ten year five percent bond drops to about eight hundred sixty dollars at seven percent, a fourteen percent loss, because more payments are locked at the old rate.
Riskier borrowers pay more. Ratings from triple A down to junk tell you how likely you are to be paid. The extra yield over a safe government bond is the credit spread.
In twenty twenty three, Silicon Valley Bank held long bonds bought when rates were low. Rates jumped, those bonds fell, and when customers pulled their money, the bank collapsed.
